items.title: The bubble before the gene
items.dek: Quanta's new series on the origin of life revisits an old, unfashionable idea: that before anything could copy itself, something had to be enclosed.
paragraphs: Most stories about how life began are stories about molecules that copy themselves. Quanta Magazine's November series on the origins of life makes room for a quieter rival, and in a piece by Perri Thaler the protagonist is not a gene at all but a wall. The starting observation is almost architectural: a modern cell runs something like a billion chemical reactions every second, and it can only do so because a membrane keeps the ingredients close together. Bruce Damer, an astrobiologist at UC Santa Cruz, argues that early chemistry faced the same problem of dilution, and that nothing much could happen until it had somewhere to gather.

The lipid-first hypothesis goes a step further than saying containers were useful; it proposes that the containers themselves were the first things to evolve. Lipids are well suited to the role, since each molecule is half drawn to water and half repelled by it, so that in water they arrange themselves into double-layered sheets that curl shut into spheres. Imagine two molecules inside such a bubble that speed up each other's production, so that the bubble grows and eventually splits, handing on roughly the same mix to its daughters. A stray third molecule slipping in plays the part of a mutation, and bubbles whose blend makes them grow faster gradually crowd out the rest.

The idea acquired its formal shape in 2000, when the geneticist Doron Lancet of the Weizmann Institute of Science and the computational biologist Daniel Segrè, now at Boston University, published a computer model in PNAS. Their simulated bubbles passed on their composition rather than a sequence, yet still varied and competed in the way natural selection requires. Damer and the biochemist David Deamer, also of UC Santa Cruz and a collaborator of the two modellers, later moved the scene to volcanic hot springs. Their hot spring hypothesis, published in Astrobiology in 2019, imagines pools drying out and refilling again and again, pressing molecules together between layers of lipid.

Not everyone is persuaded. Jack Szostak, the Nobel laureate at the University of Chicago who favours a beginning built on RNA, tells Quanta that a life made of lipids alone has never made sense to him, because no one has shown that such systems can actually evolve. He also points out that how simple lipids formed in the first place remains among the least developed parts of prebiotic chemistry, and a 2010 analysis in PNAS concluded that inheriting a rough mixture is too imprecise for selection to work on. For all his scepticism, though, Szostak grants the point on which the whole camp rests: without some kind of compartment, Darwinian evolution could not have operated.

That concession explains why Damer now says there is no longer a distinct lipid-world hypothesis. The bubble has been absorbed into almost every rival account, alongside other candidate vessels such as mineral walls of iron sulfide and coacervates, liquid droplets that hold chemistry together without any membrane. Across the series, Quanta describes a field that spent the early 2000s in bitter feuds between camps and is now being reshaped by younger researchers less attached to the question of which molecule came first.

Read with a humanist's eye, and this is interpretation rather than reporting, the debate has a familiar shape. A gene-centred story prizes the replicator, the heroic individual that reproduces itself, while the lipid story insists that nothing persists without a shared, bounded space in which relations can accumulate. Science settles such questions with evidence, not metaphors, and the evidence here is still thin. But it is worth noticing that the most stubborn dispute about our beginnings is, at bottom, an argument about whether the self or the commons came first.

items.grammar: Look at 'For all his scepticism, Szostak grants the point…'. Here 'for all + noun phrase' is concessive and means 'despite': it admits something that seems to point one way and then states a contrary result. It is more literary than 'although', often paired with 'though' or 'still' in the main clause, and the noun is usually a quality or circumstance (for all its flaws, for all their wealth).
items.grammar_zh: 注意 'For all his scepticism, Szostak grants the point…'。这里 'for all + 名词短语' 表示让步，相当于 'despite'（尽管）：先承认一个看似指向某个方向的事实，再说出相反的结果。它比 'although' 更书面，主句里常配 'though' 或 'still'，名词多为品质或情况，如 for all its flaws、for all their wealth。
questions: Why does the lipid-first hypothesis treat inheritance of composition, rather than of a sequence, as enough for natural selection, and what is the main objection to that view?
What does Szostak's concession reveal about how scientific rivals can disagree on origins yet agree on conditions?
The last paragraph reads the debate as one about 'the self or the commons'. Is this metaphor illuminating or misleading?
